TRAFFICKED | Bus ride to Hell

By: Graham Coetzer | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate cross-border human trafficking syndicates and uncover a seedy world where human beings, smuggled into SA, are treated as little more than a loaf of bread on a supermarket shelf - for s

Unique Selling Point:
We have been given exclusive information that points to a potential cross border human trafficking network transporting undocumented foreign nationals into South Africa from countries including, but not limited to Malawi, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and eSwatini.

Our main info is on the Malawi/SA side of the operation. Citizens from Malawi, are lured to SA with the promise of a new life. They are brought over by people called "the transporters" , some of who own long haul bus companies and funeral parlours. People are smuggled into South Africa by paying bribes at our borders or using false documents. Once they arrive in South Africa, undocumented foreign nationals are easy prey for traffickers. Males are often coerced into manual labour, while many females end up being sold to brothel owners. According to a case study, a brothel owner could pay as little as R3500 to the traffickers to purchase one woman. Sadly, some of them are minors.

But in an even more sinister twist, many of the victims are coerced into taking out funeral policies on themselves while on the bus ride over to SA or once they arrive here. Apparently the same people who own the transport companies, own the funeral parlours and what's known as funeral societies. In some cases they are not the same owners but have clear links to each other. The victims are told they need to take out the funeral cover in order for there bodies to bbe repatriated to Malawi if anything were to happen to them in SA.

Apparently the Malawian Consulate is aware of between 80-100 bodies being repatriated to Malawi from SA every month. Those are just the ones that are reported. They are also aware of complaints that many of these bodies have been tampered with.

Summary:
We will send in a hidden camera to see if we can prove some of the allegations, and this inssert could be part of 1 of a larger investigation.



Further information:
We have been given footage of a young Zimbabwean girl who had been smuggled into SA inside the luggage compartment of a longhaul bus.

It is suspected that she would have ended up in the hands of trafficekrs if the authorities had not saved her.

First Draft Script


INTRO

Voice
Randburg, a bustling melting pot in Jo’burg’s northern suburbs.

For migrants from countries like Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Malawi, the city is a place of dreams, a symbol of a better life. They travel here in their thousands, hoping to escape the poverty they were born into.

Link Govan
Beneath this shiny exterior, is a dark underworld. A place where human beings are smuggled, exploited and trafficked just like any other commodity. And it’s all happening right here, hidden in plain sight.

Up Sound Emma vd Walt
It’s not a break-in of a house, it’s not a hijacking. It’s a high priority crime against human beings.

Up Sound “The Agent”
I mean buying airtime in Randburg is more difficult than getting a woman.

Up Sound “Mr X”
I don’t think she was going to arrive. If we weren’t on duty that day, I don’t think today she would be alive.


ACT 1

Link Govan
In the past we’ve done so many stories on the victims of human trafficking. But this time we’re squarely focussed on the people behind the scenes, the ones that make it happen. The transporters.

Voice
These are the shadowy figures - elusive and opportunistic - who traffic people across our land borders.

Link Govan
So we’ve been filming undercover for several days now and our guy says he’s finally ready to meet us. So he’s going to bring us the footage, and tell us what he’s seen and what he’s heard.

Upsound “The Agent”

Govan: But you managed to see some things?

Agent: I managed to see lots of things.

Govan: Really?

Agent: Lots of things that I couldn’t believe with my naked eyes.

Voice
Our investigation begins after a tip off from an anonymous source.

We’re told long-haul bus companies travelling from Malawi to South Africa are being used as fronts by the transporters.

Upsound “The Agent”
Agent: Bus companies are just used as covers, because the busses are more controlled by transporters.

Govan: What’s a transporter?

Agent: A transporter, before it used to be a person who could transport goods from South Africa to a destination. Like Malawi or Zimbabwe. But now a transporter is a person who transports a human being.

Voice
It’s a secret world, a place where outsiders aren’t welcome.

To get them on camera, we send in an undercover agent to speak to some of the bus operators in the Randburg CBD. At a company called Matours, he meets this man, Josiah Soko.

Our agent tells Josiah he wants to bring a minor child, a young girl, to South Africa from Malawi.

Upsound Hidden Camera
Agent: I want a child to come here. How much will it cost?

Josiah: How old?

Agent: 6-years-old.

Josiah: 6 years. 6 years…

Voice
Not interested in why the child would be brought here, Josiah only asks about her travel documents.

Upsound Hidden Camera
Josiah: Do they have a passport?

Agent: (shakes his head)

Josiah: No passport?

Agent: (shakes head.)

Josiah: How.

Voice
Apparently suspicious of our agent, Josiah initially says no. But soon he’s making phone calls.

Upsound Hidden Camera
Josiah: A child who is six years old, how much can you charge?

Voice
He contacts a woman called Angela, and puts her on speaker phone for our agent to talk to.

Upsound Hidden Camera
Agent: Okay.

Angela: A boy or a girl?

Agent: A girl.

Voice
Angela agrees to the deal, and negotiates a price with our agent.

Upsound Hidden Camera
Agent: You just hear me over the phone, but if you could see me, I’m an old man. Can you make me a good price?

Angela: Okay we can negotiate. You can pay R5500.

Agent: R5500.

Voice
She says our agent should hand the money to Josiah.

Upsound Hidden Camera
Agent: Must I pay this man R5500?

Angela: Ja.

Voice
This transaction is based on a fiction - there is no girl travelling from Malawi - not this time.

But it’s a chilling insight into how easy it is to traffick children into a life of horror.

Upsound Emma vd Walt
Emma: So currently most of the cases in the courts are child trafficking.

Govan: Child trafficking? Into South Africa?

Emma: Yes.

Voice
Pastor, author and activist Emma van der Walt is the founder of Brave to Love - a non profit organisation assisting the victims of human trafficking.

She’s a believer in boots on the ground - often accompanying police and government agencies on raids.

Upsound Emma on raid
You must get your papers, they’re now going to send you back to Zimbabwe.

Voice
Smuggling becomes trafficking when the person brought across our borders is exploited for the financial gains of the traffickers - like being forced into the sex trade in the case of many women and children, or manual labour for men.

Upsound Emma
Govan: So is the trafficking what happens on the arrival, and smuggling the journey?

Emma: The exploitation needs to take place. So the smuggling happens, but their needs to be an exploitation that takes place against a human being for the purpose of money. Most victims are trafficked into the commercial sex trade, but we do have labour trafficking, organ trafficking, you know different forms of trafficking.


Voice
This man is a social worker and part of Emma’s team. He’s asked us to hide his identity, so we’ll call him Mr X. In November last year, he was asked to assist the police after they stopped and searched a bus on the N1 highway.

Upsound Mr X
It was coming from Zimbabwe. It had different migrants coming from different countries, including Malawi, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

Voice
Horrifyingly, a young girl was found hidden in the bus’s luggage compartment.

Upsound Mr X
Govan: She was in the luggage compartment?

Mr X: In, yes, yes.

Govan: In a box?

Mr X: In a box, and that’s how they pulled her out.

Voice
This footage of the 10 year old girl was captured just moments later.

Upsound Girl Crying Cellphone video

Upsound Mr X
She had a bag of clothes, no food, no water. I asked her when was the last time she ate? She said it was last night. I asked for her passport, it was not stamped.

Voice
It was claimed the little girl’s mother had sent her from Zimbabwe to her father in South Africa - something he later denied. In fact, she was being accompanied by a suspected transporter.

Upsound Mr X
Govan: Do you think she really was going to her dad?

Mr X: I don’t think she was going to arrive if we weren’t on duty that day, I don’t think today she would be alive.

Voice
The transporter was arrested on the same day, and the child later released into her father’s custody.

Upsound Girl Crying Cellphone video

ACT 2

Link Govan
So this bus has just arrived from Malawi. The people here say they took about three days via Mozambique, then Zimbabwe, and across the border into South Africa.

Voice
The buses arrive at this open air parking lot in central Randburg - within walking distance of the offices of operators like Matours. The area around the drop-off point is littered with rubbish

It’s a chaotic scene: As people arrive and buses and trucks are loaded with goods to be sent back across the border, others are offloaded with belongings that have been brought into the country.

Link Govan
These are not just ordinary commuters. Among them are people who have been smuggled, and others, who are being trafficked.

Voice
Either way, it’s exploitation of the poorest of the poor, on a grand scale.

Charles Luhanga came here legally from Malawi almost two decades ago. Today, his organisation Fula Africa aims to raise awareness around human trafficking.

Upsound Charles Luhanga
Charles: Especially on Malawians, we are told wrong stories to come back to South Africa.

Govan: Like what?

Charles: South Africa is good, South Africa is beautiful. Which makes vulnerable people to jump in and find themselves stranded in South Africa.

Govan: So what usually happens?

Charles: Going into jobs that you are not even supposed to do. Some women go into sex that they couldn’t even like it.

Link Govan
How much would you expect to pay for a human being? A million rand? Half a million? It’s much less. On these streets, life is cheap.

Voice
To find out, we send our undercover agent into the bus stop with a hidden camera.

Upsound Hiddencam
Agent: How are you?

Woman: I’m good.

Agent: I’m looking for a transporter. I’m Mkandawire. (Fake name)

Woman: It’s that one.

Voice
He’s introduced to this woman, Rachel Chima.

Upsound Hiddencam
Agent: I spoke to her, but what I want is secretive, I don’t know if you could help me?

Rachel: Talk to me. Sometimes something big is actually something simple.

Agent: Me, I’m not sure how to start.

Rachel: Ja, no talk.

Agent: I’ve lived here for a long time.

Voice
Our agent tells Rachel he wants a woman from Malawi. She responds that she’s returning home the next day, and can get him one.

Upsound Hiddencam
Agent: Let me ask you, because you are going, then you find me a woman.

Rachel: Okay. There is no problem.

Voice
It’s as simple as that; Rachel even refers to the potential victim as “your baby”.

Upsound Hiddencam
Agent: How do we do it?

Rachel: Give me your cellphone number. When everything is done then you talk to her. When you are ready, I will bring your “baby”.

Voice
While discussing the price, Rachel lets slip that the woman will probably be smuggled across the border.

Upsound Hiddencam
Agent: So, how much will it cost?

Rachel: First of all I’ll connect you. Then if you are satisfied, if she comes without a passport it’s K550 000. In Rand it’s R5500.

Upsound “The Agent”
Whatever you need, you can find it there. I mean buying airtime in Randburg is more difficult than getting a woman.

Voice
Our investigation into the transporters uncovered more than just their involvement in the smuggling of living human beings. Apparently, they are also making money from the dead.

Link Govan
Month end is a busy time in the Randburg CBD, with people doing their shopping. But you’ll also find thousands of Malawians, right here. But they’re not buying food or clothes, they’re paying for their funeral policies.

Voice
Our agent captures these scenes at month’s end: thousands of people gathered around the bus stop and outside the offices of the bus operators.

When the streets become too crowded, the masses spill into nearby public parks.

Malawians in South Africa gather here once a month to pay the people they refer to as the funeral societies.

Upsound Charles Luhanga
Charles: The person wanted a job, but when he arrives in South Africa he’s told you need to join a society. And those societies refer to them as funeral policies. That are not even registered anywhere

Voice
It’s a very informal system, with people handing over between R100 and R200 in cash to representatives of the various societies. In return, their names are written in a book and, in the event of their death, they’re promised their bodies will be taken home.

Upsound Charles Luhanga
From government sources, it’s quite alarming numbers of deaths per month. From 80’s to 100’s.

Voice
No one knows how many of them fell prey to traffickers. Globally, only one in a hundred victims is ever identified according to statistics.

Voice
The funeral societies seem to be raking in the cash.  But what are people getting in return?

Upsound Charles Luhanga
Families back home, they have reported that doing body viewing that side, when the bodies have reached, you cannot do body viewing because the bodies are in a very bad state.

Voice
Perhaps that’s because some of the bodies are leaving South Africa for the three day trip to Malawi packed only in caskets, on the backs of unrefrigerated trailers like these.

This footage is from Diepsloot Funeral Services, north of Jo’burg.

Upsound “The Agent”
The smell of dead bodies there. Because I could feel the smell of dead bodies.

Voice
When our agent visits them, he finds a Malawian family who’ve come to view the body of a relative.

They’re accompanied by this man, who our agent recognises as a transporter.

Upsound Agent
Govan: A transporter from the CBD?

Agent: A transporter from the Randburg CBD.

Voice
But what would transporters be doing at a funeral home?

It was time to visit Diepsloot ourselves.

Act 3
Upsound Cameras getting ready - clap

Voice
When we arrive, we’re met by Diepsloot employee Tinos Manzunzu.

Upsound
Govan: Well the bodies are arriving in a very bad state…

Tinos: Ok.

Govan: In Malawi

Tinos: Ok.

Govan: The relatives are complaining about how they are arriving, that they are not even able to open the caskets.

Tinos: Mostly what happens, some bodies come here rotten already.

Voice
Owner Elmont Gumbo arrives shortly afterwards. He tells us the bad smell our agent described may have been from decomposing bodies, like the ones they’d recently received.

Upsound Elmont Gumbo
Elmont: These bodies are already decomposed. They came when?

Govan: What the documents that you have here?

Elmont: They came when?

Man: Yesterday.

Elmont: Yesterday.

Govan: Yesterday you got decomposed bodies?

Elmont: Exactly.

Voice
Elmont tells us Diepsloot is only responsible for embalming and storing the corpses.

Upsound Elmont Gumbo
Govan: The other reason that we are here is that they are alleging that the bodies are not kept cold. So we had to come and hear for ourselves, from the business.

Elmont: We’ve got the fridges.

Voice
They offer to show us their storage facilities, and everything seems to be in order.

But guess who they say make money from delivering corpses in putrid conditions to relatives back home? The same people exploiting the poor and vulnerable along every step of the way.

Upsound Elmont Gumbo
The transporters, they’ve got their own transporters. Sometimes it takes about seven days from here to Malawi. The family of which is in Malawi, they will find the bodies rotten.

Voice
Our next stop is Matours in Randburg - where we find Josiah back on duty.

Upsound Confront
Govan: Do you own this company?

Josiah: No, I don’t own it, I’m just working here.

Govan: Why is this company being used to smuggle children across the border?

Josiah: On that issue, because on that issue I don’t know

Govan: No, you must know about it. You’re the one. You are facilitating the smuggling of children, without documentation, across the border.

Voice
When we show him the hidden camera footage, he suddenly changes his tune.

Upsound Confront
Josiah: Yes this is me.

Govan: That’s you.

Josiah: We don’t know each other.

Govan: And yet you gave him the number of someone to organise for the transport of a child without paperwork. For smuggling my brother. You just sit there in your chair, smiling. That’s not good enough my brother. I don’t understand why you are looking so disappointed in yourself.

Josiah: Ja, because I have no idea what is going on.

Govan: You’re lying, you know exactly what’s going on. You’re lying. You knew exactly who to call to get the child across. Don’t take me for a fool man.

Josiah: I cannot take you for a fool.

Voice
We search for Rachel Chima, but apparently she’s back in Malawi, so we phone her.

Upsound Rachel phone call.
Govan: You are a transporter, from Malawi?

Rachel: Yes you are, we’ve got you on camera. You are on hidden camera footage. We recorded you.

PUTS PHONE DOWN

Voice
A story as dark as this one holds a stark lesson: we have a long way to go to end the scourge of human trafficking - if that’s even possible.

Upsound Emma
Emma: The trafficking in Persons Global Report gives a yearly report on what South Africa’s doing and we’ve been downgraded once again last year.

Govan: Really?

Emma: And we haven’t got the TIP report for this year but last year we downgraded again because we’re not even reaching the standard of what we need to reach in fighting human trafficking.

Voice
As of today, there are no reliable statistics available for the scale of the problem in the country. How many victims are out there right now, remains anyone’s guess.

But this time we’re squarely focussed on the people behind the scenes, the ones that make it happen. The transporters. Voice These are the shadowy figures - elusive and opportunistic - who traffic people across our land borders. Link Govan So we’ve been filming undercover for several days now and our guy says he’s finally ready to meet us. So he’s going to bring us the footage, and tell us what he’s seen and what he’s heard. Upsound “The Agent” Govan: But you managed to see some things? Agent: I managed to see lots of things. Govan: Really? Agent: Lots of things that I couldn’t believe with my naked eyes. Voice Our investigation begins after a tip off from an anonymous source. We’re told long-haul bus companies travelling from Malawi to South Africa are being used as fronts by the transporters. Upsound “The Agent” Agent: Bus companies are just used as covers, because the busses are more controlled by transporters. Govan: What’s a transporter? Agent: A transporter, before it used to be a person who could transport goods from South Africa to a destination. Like Malawi or Zimbabwe. But now a transporter is a person who transports a human being. Voice It’s a secret world, a place where outsiders aren’t welcome. To get them on camera, we send in an undercover agent to speak to some of the bus operators in the Randburg CBD. At a company called Matours, he meets this man, Josiah Soko. Our agent tells Josiah he wants to bring a minor child, a young girl, to South Africa from Malawi. Upsound Hidden Camera Agent: I want a child to come here. How much will it cost? Josiah: How old? Agent: 6-years-old. Josiah: 6 years. 6 years… Voice Not interested in why the child would be brought here, Josiah only asks about her travel documents. Upsound Hidden Camera Josiah: Do they have a passport? Agent: (shakes his head) Josiah: No passport? Agent: (shakes head.) Josiah: How. Voice Apparently suspicious of our agent, Josiah initially says no. But soon he’s making phone calls. Upsound Hidden Camera Josiah: A child who is six years old, how much can you charge? Voice He contacts a woman called Angela, and puts her on speaker phone for our agent to talk to. Upsound Hidden Camera Agent: Okay. Angela: A boy or a girl? Agent: A girl. Voice Angela agrees to the deal, and negotiates a price with our agent. Upsound Hidden Camera Agent: You just hear me over the phone, but if you could see me, I’m an old man. Can you make me a good price? Angela: Okay we can negotiate. You can pay R5500. Agent: R5500. Voice She says our agent should hand the money to Josiah. Upsound Hidden Camera Agent: Must I pay this man R5500? Angela: Ja. Voice This transaction is based on a fiction - there is no girl travelling from Malawi - not this time. But it’s a chilling insight into how easy it is to traffick children into a life of horror. Upsound Emma vd Walt Emma: So currently most of the cases in the courts are child trafficking. Govan: Child trafficking? Into South Africa? Emma: Yes. Voice Pastor, author and activist Emma van der Walt is the founder of Brave to Love - a non profit organisation assisting the victims of human trafficking. She’s a believer in boots on the ground - often accompanying police and government agencies on raids. Upsound Emma on raid You must get your papers, they’re now going to send you back to Zimbabwe. Voice Smuggling becomes trafficking when the person brought across our borders is exploited for the financial gains of the traffickers - like being forced into the sex trade in the case of many women and children, or manual labour for men. Upsound Emma Govan: So is the trafficking what happens on the arrival, and smuggling the journey? Emma: The exploitation needs to take place. So the smuggling happens, but their needs to be an exploitation that takes place against a human being for the purpose of money. Most victims are trafficked into the commercial sex trade, but we do have labour trafficking, organ trafficking, you know different forms of trafficking. Voice This man is a social worker and part of Emma’s team. He’s asked us to hide his identity, so we’ll call him Mr X. In November last year, he was asked to assist the police after they stopped and searched a bus on the N1 highway. Upsound Mr X It was coming from Zimbabwe. It had different migrants coming from different countries, including Malawi, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. Voice Horrifyingly, a young girl was found hidden in the bus’s luggage compartment. Upsound Mr X Govan: She was in the luggage compartment? Mr X: In, yes, yes. Govan: In a box? Mr X: In a box, and that’s how they pulled her out. Voice This footage of the 10 year old girl was captured just moments later. Upsound Girl Crying Cellphone video Upsound Mr X She had a bag of clothes, no food, no water. I asked her when was the last time she ate? She said it was last night. I asked for her passport, it was not stamped. Voice It was claimed the little girl’s mother had sent her from Zimbabwe to her father in South Africa - something he later denied. In fact, she was being accompanied by a suspected transporter. Upsound Mr X Govan: Do you think she really was going to her dad? Mr X: I don’t think she was going to arrive if we weren’t on duty that day, I don’t think today she would be alive. Voice The transporter was arrested on the same day, and the child later released into her father’s custody. Upsound Girl Crying Cellphone video ACT 2 Link Govan So this bus has just arrived from Malawi. The people here say they took about three days via Mozambique, then Zimbabwe, and across the border into South Africa. Voice The buses arrive at this open air parking lot in central Randburg - within walking distance of the offices of operators like Matours. The area around the drop-off point is littered with rubbish It’s a chaotic scene: As people arrive and buses and trucks are loaded with goods to be sent back across the border, others are offloaded with belongings that have been brought into the country. Link Govan These are not just ordinary commuters. Among them are people who have been smuggled, and others, who are being trafficked. Voice Either way, it’s exploitation of the poorest of the poor, on a grand scale. Charles Luhanga came here legally from Malawi almost two decades ago. Today, his organisation Fula Africa aims to raise awareness around human trafficking. Upsound Charles Luhanga Charles: Especially on Malawians, we are told wrong stories to come back to South Africa. Govan: Like what? Charles: South Africa is good, South Africa is beautiful. Which makes vulnerable people to jump in and find themselves stranded in South Africa. Govan: So what usually happens? Charles: Going into jobs that you are not even supposed to do. Some women go into sex that they couldn’t even like it. Link Govan How much would you expect to pay for a human being? A million rand? Half a million? It’s much less. On these streets, life is cheap. Voice To find out, we send our undercover agent into the bus stop with a hidden camera. Upsound Hiddencam Agent: How are you? Woman: I’m good. Agent: I’m looking for a transporter. I’m Mkandawire. (Fake name) Woman: It’s that one. Voice He’s introduced to this woman, Rachel Chima. Upsound Hiddencam Agent: I spoke to her, but what I want is secretive, I don’t know if you could help me? Rachel: Talk to me. Sometimes something big is actually something simple. Agent: Me, I’m not sure how to start. Rachel: Ja, no talk. Agent: I’ve lived here for a long time. Voice Our agent tells Rachel he wants a woman from Malawi. She responds that she’s returning home the next day, and can get him one. Upsound Hiddencam Agent: Let me ask you, because you are going, then you find me a woman. Rachel: Okay. There is no problem. Voice It’s as simple as that; Rachel even refers to the potential victim as “your baby”. Upsound Hiddencam Agent: How do we do it? Rachel: Give me your cellphone number. When everything is done then you talk to her. When you are ready, I will bring your “baby”. Voice While discussing the price, Rachel lets slip that the woman will probably be smuggled across the border. Upsound Hiddencam Agent: So, how much will it cost? Rachel: First of all I’ll connect you. Then if you are satisfied, if she comes without a passport it’s K550 000. In Rand it’s R5500. Upsound “The Agent” Whatever you need, you can find it there. I mean buying airtime in Randburg is more difficult than getting a woman. Voice Our investigation into the transporters uncovered more than just their involvement in the smuggling of living human beings. Apparently, they are also making money from the dead. Link Govan Month end is a busy time in the Randburg CBD, with people doing their shopping. But you’ll also find thousands of Malawians, right here. But they’re not buying food or clothes, they’re paying for their funeral policies. Voice Our agent captures these scenes at month’s end: thousands of people gathered around the bus stop and outside the offices of the bus operators. When the streets become too crowded, the masses spill into nearby public parks. Malawians in South Africa gather here once a month to pay the people they refer to as the funeral societies. Upsound Charles Luhanga Charles: The person wanted a job, but when he arrives in South Africa he’s told you need to join a society. And those societies refer to them as funeral policies. That are not even registered anywhere Voice It’s a very informal system, with people handing over between R100 and R200 in cash to representatives of the various societies. In return, their names are written in a book and, in the event of their death, they’re promised their bodies will be taken home. Upsound Charles Luhanga From government sources, it’s quite alarming numbers of deaths per month. From 80’s to 100’s. Voice No one knows how many of them fell prey to traffickers. Globally, only one in a hundred victims is ever identified according to statistics. Voice The funeral societies seem to be raking in the cash. But what are people getting in return? Upsound Charles Luhanga Families back home, they have reported that doing body viewing that side, when the bodies have reached, you cannot do body viewing because the bodies are in a very bad state. Voice Perhaps that’s because some of the bodies are leaving South Africa for the three day trip to Malawi packed only in caskets, on the backs of unrefrigerated trailers like these. This footage is from Diepsloot Funeral Services, north of Jo’burg. Upsound “The Agent” The smell of dead bodies there. Because I could feel the smell of dead bodies. Voice When our agent visits them, he finds a Malawian family who’ve come to view the body of a relative. They’re accompanied by this man, who our agent recognises as a transporter. Upsound Agent Govan: A transporter from the CBD? Agent: A transporter from the Randburg CBD. Voice But what would transporters be doing at a funeral home? It was time to visit Diepsloot ourselves. Act 3 Upsound Cameras getting ready - clap Voice When we arrive, we’re met by Diepsloot employee Tinos Manzunzu. Upsound Govan: Well the bodies are arriving in a very bad state… Tinos: Ok. Govan: In Malawi Tinos: Ok. Govan: The relatives are complaining about how they are arriving, that they are not even able to open the caskets. Tinos: Mostly what happens, some bodies come here rotten already. Voice Owner Elmont Gumbo arrives shortly afterwards. He tells us the bad smell our agent described may have been from decomposing bodies, like the ones they’d recently received. Upsound Elmont Gumbo Elmont: These bodies are already decomposed. They came when? Govan: What the documents that you have here? Elmont: They came when? Man: Yesterday. Elmont: Yesterday. Govan: Yesterday you got decomposed bodies? Elmont: Exactly. Voice Elmont tells us Diepsloot is only responsible for embalming and storing the corpses. Upsound Elmont Gumbo Govan: The other reason that we are here is that they are alleging that the bodies are not kept cold. So we had to come and hear for ourselves, from the business. Elmont: We’ve got the fridges. Voice They offer to show us their storage facilities, and everything seems to be in order. But guess who they say make money from delivering corpses in putrid conditions to relatives back home? The same people exploiting the poor and vulnerable along every step of the way. Upsound Elmont Gumbo The transporters, they’ve got their own transporters. Sometimes it takes about seven days from here to Malawi. The family of which is in Malawi, they will find the bodies rotten. Voice Our next stop is Matours in Randburg - where we find Josiah back on duty. Upsound Confront Govan: Do you own this company? Josiah: No, I don’t own it, I’m just working here. Govan: Why is this company being used to smuggle children across the border? Josiah: On that issue, because on that issue I don’t know Govan: No, you must know about it. You’re the one. You are facilitating the smuggling of children, without documentation, across the border. Voice When we show him the hidden camera footage, he suddenly changes his tune. Upsound Confront Josiah: Yes this is me. Govan: That’s you. Josiah: We don’t know each other. Govan: And yet you gave him the number of someone to organise for the transport of a child without paperwork. For smuggling my brother. You just sit there in your chair, smiling. That’s not good enough my brother. I don’t understand why you are looking so disappointed in yourself. Josiah: Ja, because I have no idea what is going on. Govan: You’re lying, you know exactly what’s going on. You’re lying. You knew exactly who to call to get the child across. Don’t take me for a fool man. Josiah: I cannot take you for a fool. Voice We search for Rachel Chima, but apparently she’s back in Malawi, so we phone her. Upsound Rachel phone call. Govan: You are a transporter, from Malawi? Rachel: Yes you are, we’ve got you on camera. You are on hidden camera footage. We recorded you. PUTS PHONE DOWN Voice A story as dark as this one holds a stark lesson: we have a long way to go to end the scourge of human trafficking - if that’s even possible. Upsound Emma Emma: The trafficking in Persons Global Report gives a yearly report on what South Africa’s doing and we’ve been downgraded once again last year. Govan: Really? Emma: And we haven’t got the TIP report for this year but last year we downgraded again because we’re not even reaching the standard of what we need to reach in fighting human trafficking. Voice As of today, there are no reliable statistics available for the scale of the problem in the country. How many victims are out there right now, remains anyone’s guess. PROMO2 Voice A ten year old girl is smuggled across our borders - kept without food and water in the luggage compartment of a bus. Upsound Girl crying Voice Saved by the authorities, she is one of the lucky ones. Up Sound “Mr X” I don’t think she was going to arrive. If we weren’t on duty that day, I don’t think today she would be alive. 7 sec PROMO3 VO We investigate cross border trafficking, where hundreds of undocumented foreign nationals are smuggled into South Africa. Emma It’s not a break-in of a house, it’s not a hijacking. It’s a high priority crime against human beings. 5 Sec Voice And uncover a secret world hidden in plain sight on the streets of Joburg. Upsound agent Agent: I managed to see lots of things. Govan: Really? Agent: Lots of things that I couldn’t believe with my naked eyes. PROMO4 VO We investigate cross border smuggling and uncover a seedy world where human beings, smuggled into SA, are treated as little more than a loaf of bread on a supermarket shelf. Upsound girl crying VO On the streets of Johannesburg, life is sometimes cheap. Upsound Govan You are facilitating the smuggling of children without documentation over the border. 6.14 sec PROMO5 VO Alleged cross border human trafficking networks operating inside of South Africa Sound Up Emma I can tell you we have a massive problem on our hands. VO Behind it all, the middlemen known simply as the transporters. Upsound Govan You’re lying! You knew exactly who to call to get the child across.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We investigate cross-border human trafficking syndicates and uncover a seedy world where human beings, smuggled into SA, are treated as little more than a loaf of bread on a supermarket shelf - for s
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have been given exclusive information that points to a potential cross border human trafficking network transporting undocumented foreign nationals into South Africa from countries including, but not limited to Malawi, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and eSwatini. Our main info is on the Malawi/SA side of the operation. Citizens from Malawi, are lured to SA with the promise of a new life. They are brought over by people called "the transporters" , some of who own long haul bus companies and funeral parlours. People are smuggled into South Africa by paying bribes at our borders or using false documents. Once they arrive in South Africa, undocumented foreign nationals are easy prey for traffickers. Males are often coerced into manual labour, while many females end up being sold to brothel owners. According to a case study, a brothel owner could pay as little as R3500 to the traffickers to purchase one woman. Sadly, some of them are minors. But in an even more sinister twist, many of the victims are coerced into taking out funeral policies on themselves while on the bus ride over to SA or once they arrive here. Apparently the same people who own the transport companies, own the funeral parlours and what's known as funeral societies. In some cases they are not the same owners but have clear links to each other. The victims are told they need to take out the funeral cover in order for there bodies to bbe repatriated to Malawi if anything were to happen to them in SA. Apparently the Malawian Consulate is aware of between 80-100 bodies being repatriated to Malawi from SA every month. Those are just the ones that are reported. They are also aware of complaints that many of these bodies have been tampered with.
metadata.Summary: We will send in a hidden camera to see if we can prove some of the allegations, and this inssert could be part of 1 of a larger investigation.
metadata.Further information: We have been given footage of a young Zimbabwean girl who had been smuggled into SA inside the luggage compartment of a longhaul bus. It is suspected that she would have ended up in the hands of trafficekrs if the authorities had not saved her.
